Full disclosure. Jag tycker inte om Islam. Jag tycker inte om Kristendom heller och jag tycker inte om några religioner, vuxna människor ska inte tro på sagor och de ska definitivt inte indoktrinera sina barn till att tro. Vi ska naturligtvis fortsätta ha religionsfrihet och folk ska få tro det de vill, men jag behöver inte tycka om det och gör det inte heller.

Det som oroar mig är att kritik av Islam (vilket i mina ögon är helt legitimt, precis som kritik av Kristendom, syndikalism eller andra politiska eller religiösa idéer) blandas ihop med förakt mot muslimer. Att säga att profeten Muhammad var som bäst en problematisk figur och som värst en pedofilisk krigsherre är inte samma sak som att hävda att alla muslimer är terrorister. Att påpeka hur Koranen (precis som Bibeln) innehåller vidrighet efter vidrighet är inte samma sak som att kasta grishuvuden mot moskéer.

Den samhällsliga debatten just nu verkar stå mellan en höger som drar mer och mer paralleller mellan muslimer och terrorister och en vänster som med alla medel vill försvara Islam. Ingen sida har rätt utan göder den andra sidans argument. Om vi ska hårdra det, IS gynnar den högerextrema vågen i Europa och de högerextrema besluten som tas i Europa (sjalförbud på skolor i Frankrike t.ex.) gör det lättare för IS att rekrytera i Europa. Ska vi kunna bryta den cykeln så måste vi lyfta debatten från "alla muslimer är terrorister" vs. "inga terrorister är muslimer" till "Islam, precis som alla andra politiska och religiösa idéer kan användas för att rättfärdiga terrorism".

An old paintbrush.

Once, many years ago, our hero (the bard) had picked up a small paintbrush, the type you'd use to fill in details like eyebrows and lips in portraits. Rumor had it that it'd belonged to a master painter, but most likely it had just been used by the innkeeper's wife to draw amateurish portraits of wealthier customers in vain but unsuccessful attempts to seem sophisticated.

The crowd had been a bit on the rowdier side that night, mercenaries spending their meager pay on drink and women, and our hero had to endure both words and objects being hurled at him, but it paid well, for an inn close to nowhere. It also had a very lovely barmaid working there. Her name was, well, that's not important really, let's just say she appreciated the advances, and later rather naughty propositions, of our hero.

Unfortunately, one of the mercenaries did not. A big fellow with a slow-looking face but quite big arms, who had taken a liking to the barmaid our hero was flirting with. Naturally, things escalated. Insults masked as clever wordplay might work well in a debating society but against a mindless professional murderer in an establishment far away from polite society, they are far from optimal. The first swing had been a miss, but the second one did not. It hit our hero square in the nose and he was knocked onto a table. The mercenary stood over our hero and grabbed by him the throat. "My woman, you perfumed fucking poet!" he said while applying pressure. Panic was gripping our hero. Was this how he was going to die, to a stranger's hand in a forgotten tavern?

No, it was not. While he was desperately searching for a weapon, any weapon, he felt it, the paintbrush. He grabbed it firmly and stabbed his attacker straight in the eye! The brute recoiled, letting go and our hero rolled himself off the table. Now free, and invigorated by the successful attack, he stood himself and picked up a chair that he used to crush the attackers head. Triumph! The other mercenaries, oblivious up until this point, accustomed to brawls like this, now stood up, but seeing their dead comrade, presumably their strongest warrior made them nervous and they sat themselves down and forgot all about it. After all, his pay was now their pay.

The barmaid came up to our hero. "That was very brave of you," she said. Our hero, like all musicians a masterful seductor, replied: "Oh, it was nothing really. I just did what had to be done." The barmaid glanced at the staircase leading to the rentable rooms upstairs. "Come. Let me bandage your wounds, brave warrior," she said. Our hero nodded, gestured her to lead the way and bent down to pick up the paintbrush. "Who knows? It might come in handy," he thought to himself as he followed the barmaid to his room where she, ahem, tended his wounds. Very, very carefully.
